---
title: "Phylogenetic tree of *Sarcoptes scabiei* sequences from human hosts"
format:
  html:
    fig-width: 10
    fig-height: 9
---

## Aim

The sheet `.github/Sarcoptes_human_accessions.csv` lists representative GenBank
accessions for *Sarcoptes scabiei* (itch mite) protein sequences sampled from
**human** hosts. Each row is one "cluster" of near-identical sequences; the
column `n (sequences in cluster)` says how many sequences the cluster stood in
for (cluster sizes were read by eye from a figure, so they are approximate).

Here we turn those accessions into a **phylogenetic tree** ("who is related to
whom") in four steps:

1. Download the 64 protein sequences from NCBI using the accessions.
2. Keep only the **COI** sequences (cytochrome oxidase subunit I, the standard
   mite barcoding gene) — these are the sequences that are biologically
   comparable to each other.
3. Align the COI sequences with **MAFFT**.
4. Build a **neighbour-joining tree** with **ape**, and measure how reliable
   each branch is with a **bootstrap**.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(here)
  library(Biostrings)  # reads FASTA files
  library(ape)         # tree building (nj, dist.aa, boot.phylo)
})
```

## Read the accession sheet

The sheet uses old Mac-style line breaks (`\r`), which `read.csv()` handles
automatically. Rows at the bottom (Total, notes) are dropped by keeping rows
with a non-empty accession.

```{r accessions}
x <- read.csv(here(".github", "Sarcoptes_human_accessions.csv"))
x <- x[x$Representative.accession != "" & !is.na(x$Representative.accession), ]
colnames(x)[4] <- "n_cluster"
nrow(x)
```

`r nrow(x)` representative accessions in total.

## Download the sequences from NCBI

One call to NCBI's `efetch` service fetches all sequences as FASTA. The file is
cached on disk, so re-rendering this document does not re-download it.

```{r fetch, cache=FALSE}
fa <- here("group_project", "sarcoptes_human.fasta")
if (!file.exists(fa)) {
  url <- sprintf(
    "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=protein&id=%s&rettype=fasta&retmode=text",
    paste(x$Representative.accession, collapse = ","))
  download.file(url, fa, mode = "wb")
}
seqs <- readAAStringSet(fa)  # a named vector of protein sequences
length(seqs)
```

For the circular all-sequences figure later, we also align **all 64**
sequences (cached, like everything else):

```{r align-all}
human_aln_fa <- here("group_project", "sarcoptes_human.aln.fasta")
if (!file.exists(human_aln_fa)) {
  status <- system2("mafft", c("--auto", "--quiet", fa), stdout = human_aln_fa)
  stopifnot(status == 0)
}
cat("full alignment cached at", basename(human_aln_fa), "\n")
```

## Keep only COI

```{r coi-count}
head(names(seqs), 3)
```

```{r coi-subset}
is_coi <- grepl("cytochrome (c )?oxidase subunit I", names(seqs)) &
          !grepl("subunit II", names(seqs))
cat("COI sequences:", sum(is_coi),
    "| other proteins:", sum(!is_coi), "\n")
```

The other `r sum(!is_coi)` sequences are assorted proteins — allergens
(Sar s 1), paramyosin, myosin, a sodium channel, a trypsin-like protease and
so on. They are *different genes*, so they cannot be meaningfully compared
against COI and are left out of the tree (listed in the appendix).

```{r write-coi}
coi_fa     <- here("group_project", "sarcoptes_coi.fasta")
coi_aln_fa <- here("group_project", "sarcoptes_coi.aln.fasta")
writeXStringSet(seqs[is_coi], coi_fa)
```

## Align with MAFFT

MAFFT (Multiple Alignment using Fast Fourier Transform) lines the sequences up
so that matching amino acids sit in the same column. `--auto` lets MAFFT pick
a sensible strategy for the dataset size.

```{r mafft}
if (!file.exists(coi_aln_fa)) {
  status <- system2("mafft", c("--auto", "--quiet", coi_fa), stdout = coi_aln_fa)
  stopifnot(status == 0)
}
aln <- as.matrix(readAAStringSet(coi_aln_fa))
dim(aln)  # sequences x aligned positions
```

## Build the tree (neighbour joining + bootstrap)

**Neighbour joining** builds the tree by repeatedly joining the two sequences
that look most different-overall, using pairwise amino-acid distances
(`dist.aa`, a Dayhoff-style protein distance). It is fast and standard for a
first look; a more rigorous option would be maximum likelihood.

The **bootstrap** (100 replicates) re-runs the analysis on randomly resampled
alignment columns. A branch supported in ≥70% of replicates is usually
considered solid.

```{r tree}
d  <- dist.aa(aln, pairwise = TRUE)   # handles gapped columns pair by pair
tr <- ladderize(nj(d))

# shorter tip labels: accession + cluster size, e.g. "WHU50584.1 (n=105)"
acc_of <- sub(" .*", "", names(seqs)[is_coi])
nmap <- setNames(x$n_cluster, x$Representative.accession)
tr$tip.label <- paste0(acc_of, " (n=", nmap[acc_of], ")")

# bootstrap support for each internal branch
bs <- boot.phylo(ladderize(nj(d)), aln,
                 function(z) nj(dist.aa(z, pairwise = TRUE)),
                 B = 100, trees = FALSE)
bs[is.na(bs)] <- 0  # the root position has no bootstrap value
tr$node.label <- bs
```

```{r tree-plot, fig.cap="Figure 1. Neighbour-joining tree of the 43 COI protein sequences of *Sarcoptes scabiei* from human hosts.", fig.dpi=300}
write.tree(tr, here("group_project", "sarcoptes_coi.nwk"))
plot(tr, type = "phylogram", cex = 0.65, label.offset = 0.004, no.margin = TRUE)
n <- length(tr$tip.label)
# bootstrap numbers at each branch point, green when solid
nodelabels(text = as.character(tr$node.label), node = (n + 1):(n + tr$Nnode),
           frame = "none", cex = 0.5, adj = c(0.5, -0.3),
           col = ifelse(tr$node.label >= 70, "darkgreen", "grey45"))
add.scale.bar(length = 0.1)  # 0.1 = 10% amino-acid difference
title(main = "Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis — database retrieved 531 proteins",
      sub  = "43 COI representatives · neighbour joining on Dayhoff protein distances · bootstrap support (green = ≥ 70%)",
      cex.sub = 0.8, line = 0.5)
```

## Circular view of all 64 sequences

For completeness, the **full set of 64 sequences** (COI plus the other
proteins) drawn as a **circular cladogram** — same grouping logic as above
(neighbour joining), but drawn in a circle with equal-length branches so all
64 labels stay readable. Six accessions of interest are highlighted in their
own colours; everything else is grey. Because the tips here are a mix of
different genes, the branch arrangement mostly reflects *which protein* a
sequence is, not mite ancestry — this figure is for spotting individual
accessions, not for reading evolution off.

```{r circular-tree}
# full 64-sequence alignment (already produced when every sequence was
# downloaded and aligned before the COI subset was made)
aln64 <- as.matrix(readAAStringSet(here("group_project", "sarcoptes_human.aln.fasta")))
d64  <- dist.aa(aln64, pairwise = TRUE)
tr64 <- ladderize(nj(d64))
acc64 <- sub(" .*", "", tr64$tip.label)
tr64$tip.label <- paste0(acc64, " (n=", nmap[acc64], ")")

hi  <- c("AAS93675.1", "AAS93667.1", "AAS93669.1",
         "AAO15606.1", "AAO15613.1", "CAL18242.1")
pal <- c("red", "darkorange3", "purple",
         "dodgerblue3", "forestgreen", "magenta")
names(pal) <- hi
tipcol <- ifelse(acc64 %in% hi, pal[acc64], "black")  # black = easier to read in print
stopifnot(!any(is.na(tipcol)))  # all six must be present in the 64
```

```{r}
#| label: circular-plot
#| fig.cap: "Figure 2. Circular cladogram of all 64 Sarcoptes scabiei protein sequences from human hosts."
#| fig.dpi: 300
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10
plot(tr64, type = "fan", use.edge.length = FALSE, cex = 0.68, font = 2,
     tip.color = tipcol, show.node.label = FALSE, edge.width = 1.1,
     rotate = 20)
legend("bottomleft", legend = hi, col = pal, pch = 16, pt.cex = 1.4,
       cex = 0.95, bty = "n", title = "highlighted accessions")
title(main = "Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis — database retrieved 531 proteins (all 64 representatives)",
      cex.main = 1.15)
```

> **Figure 2. Circular cladogram of all 64 representative protein sequences
> from *Sarcoptes scabiei* var. *hominis* (database retrieved 531 proteins).** Neighbour joining on
> Dayhoff protein distances, drawn with equal-length branches (a cladogram) in
> a circular layout so that all labels are legible. Each labelled accession
> stands in for a cluster of near-identical sequences (cluster size in
> brackets). The six highlighted accessions are AAS93675.1 (red), AAS93667.1
> (orange), AAS93669.1 (purple), AAO15606.1 (blue), AAO15613.1 (green) and
> CAL18242.1 (magenta). Because the set mixes different genes, the grouping
> mainly separates protein types (COI vs allergens vs muscle proteins, etc.)
> and should not be read as a species phylogeny. **Tree scale:** not
> applicable — branches are drawn with equal lengths for legibility, so only
> the grouping (topology), not distances, is informative in this figure.

## Caption for Figure 1

> **Figure 1. Neighbour-joining phylogeny of mitochondrial COI protein
> sequences from *Sarcoptes scabiei* var. *hominis* sampled from human
> hosts (database retrieved 531 proteins; 43 COI representatives shown).**
> The 43 representative COI accessions from `.github/Sarcoptes_human_accessions.csv`
> were downloaded from NCBI, aligned with MAFFT (`--auto`), and their amino-acid
> distances used to build an unrooted neighbour-joining tree with ape. Tip
> labels give the GenBank accession and, in brackets, how many near-identical
> sequences the representative stood for (cluster sizes read by eye from the
> source figure). Numbers at internal nodes are bootstrap support from 100
> resamplings of alignment columns; green values (≥ 70%) indicate well
> supported groups. **Tree scale:** branch lengths are in substitutions per
> amino-acid site; the scale bar corresponds to 0.1. Because each sequence is
> a partial fragment (40–275 amino acids) and many deep branches have low
> support, the tree should be read as a first-pass clustering of the available
> human-host COI sequences rather than a definitive mite phylogeny.

## Description of this work

**What a phylogenetic tree is.** A tree is a hypothesis about ancestry: tips
that join close together share a more recent common ancestor than tips that
join far apart. Branch length is proportional to how much the sequences differ.

**What we did, in plain words.**

1. The sheet lists one representative accession per cluster of near-identical
   sequences — 64 representatives standing in for 531 sequences (the sheet's
   own note says 532 was the intended total; a small reading error, harmless
   here since we only use the representatives).
2. From NCBI we pulled the protein sequence behind each accession. Inspection
   showed they are **not all the same gene**: 43 are mitochondrial **COI**
   (the mite barcoding gene) and 21 are unrelated proteins (allergens,
   muscle proteins, detoxification enzymes, etc.).
3. Because only same-gene sequences are comparable, we kept the 43 COI ones.
   MAFFT lined them up (283 aligned columns).
4. `dist.aa()` summarised each pair of sequences as one distance (roughly:
   how many amino-acid positions differ, corrected for invisible changes),
   and neighbour joining turned those distances into the tree.
5. The bootstrap asks: if we resample the alignment columns, does the same
   group keep appearing? Groups that survive ≥ 70% of resamplings are drawn
   in green above.

**What the tree shows.** Most human-host COI sequences sit on long branches
with weak deep support — consistent with a diverse set of mites collected from
many patients. A few tight clusters with high support (e.g. the accession
pairs around QIK02… and WKB12…) are groups of nearly identical sequences.
The exact membership of deeper clusters is not resolved by these short
fragments; more (or longer) sequences would be needed for that.

**Caveats, honestly stated.**

- Sequences are short partial fragments (40–275 aa); short alignments give
  shaky support values, which is exactly what we see.
- `dist.aa` treats gaps pair by pair (`pairwise = TRUE`); with fragments of
  different lengths, pairs only share part of the alignment.
- The tree is unrooted — it shows relatedness but does not say which lineage
  is "oldest".
- This is a protein-level tree of a mitochondrial gene sampled **only from
  human hosts**; it cannot speak to mites on other animals (dogs, pigs,
  wildlife), so it is not evidence about cross-host transmission.

**How you could check this yourself.** Pick any two tips joined at a green
node — e.g. WHU50584.1 and its neighbour — and BLAST one against the other at
<https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov> ("blastp"): near-identical sequences will
report ~100% identity, which is the tree's claim, checked independently. You
can also re-render this document after deleting
`group_project/sarcoptes_coi.aln.fasta` to confirm MAFFT gives the same
alignment twice.

## Appendix: accessions excluded (non-COI proteins)

```{r excluded}
data.frame(protein = sub("^[^ ]+ ", "", names(seqs)[!is_coi]),
           accession = sub(" .*", "", names(seqs)[!is_coi]))
```

## Choices made

- Kept only COI sequences for the tree — alternative: build one tree of all 64
  sequences, which mixes unrelated genes and produces a meaningless jumble of
  long branches.
- Amino-acid (protein) distances with `dist.aa`, Dayhoff-type correction —
  alternative: convert back to nucleotides and use `dist.dna` (K80), but we
  only had protein sequences.
- Neighbour joining — alternative: maximum likelihood (more rigorous, much
  slower; overkill for a first look at 43 short fragments).
- MAFFT `--auto` alignment — alternative: ClustalW, generally less accurate.
- Gaps handled pairwise in the distance — alternative: strip all gapped
  columns first, which would discard most of this short alignment.
- 100 bootstrap replicates, ≥ 70% considered solid — alternative: 1,000
  replicates (tighter support estimates, ~10× slower).
- Tree left unrooted (no outgroup available: no non-human-host COI sequence in
  the sheet) — alternative: midpoint rooting, which assumes the two most
  distant sequences bracket the root and can be misleading.
- Cluster sizes shown in the tip labels as `(n=…)` — alternative: drawing tip
  circles whose size scales with `n`, prettier but harder to read exact values.
- Cluster sizes taken as given from the sheet (read by eye from a figure) —
  alternative: re-export the collapse table for exact counts.
- Figure 2 drawn as a **circular cladogram** with equal-length branches —
  alternative: keep real branch lengths (a distance fan), which is more
  faithful but unreadable here because the unrelated proteins sit on extremely
  long branches that squash the COI cluster into a sliver.
- Non-highlighted tips in plain grey, each highlighted accession in its own
  colour — alternative: one single colour for all six, or scaling the colour
  brightness by cluster size.
